Conormal Sheaf (Morphisms of Schemes, Stacks Project)

The initial part of this inquiry refers to Lemma 33.2 from the chapter "Morphisms of Schemes" of the Stacks Project. In particular, if $i: Z \rightarrow X$ is an embedding and $\mathcal{I}$ is the corresponding ideal sheaf, then the conormal sheaf is $C_{Z/X} = i^*(\mathcal{I})$. What i don't perceive is why $i^*(\mathcal{I}) = i^{-1}(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2)$. My attempts: if i apply the definition of the pullback $i^*$ i get $i^*(\mathcal{I}) = i^{-1} \mathcal{I} \otimes_{i^{-1}O_X} O_Z$. Additionally, i also observe that if $R$ is a ring and $I$ some ideal then $I/I^2 = I \times_R R/I$. But i am struggling to merge these two facts to obtain $i^{-1}(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2)$.

By definition, we have $ i^*(\mathcal{I}) = i^{-1}(\mathcal{I})\otimes _{i^{-1}\mathcal O_X} \mathcal O_Z$. On the other hand $\mathcal O_Z=i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I)$, so that $$ i^*(\mathcal{I}) = i^{-1}(\mathcal{I})\otimes _{i^{-1}\mathcal O_X} i^{-1}(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I)=i^{-1}[\mathcal I\otimes _{\mathcal O_X} \mathcal O_X/\mathcal I]=i^{-1}[\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2]$$ just as is stated in the Stacks Project.

perturbations.a:
Harmonic function.

The function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x) = \|x\|^{2-n}$, where $\|~\|$ signifies the Euclidean norm, is harmonic. This is merely a straightforward computation.

My question is: why should we anticipate this function to be harmonic? In other words, if someone inquired whether this function is harmonic or not, what type of reasoning could lead you to suggest that this is the case, before actually calculating its laplacian?

I'm just attempting to grasp the intuition behind harmonic functions. Since this can be a little unclear, I'm willing to accept alternative proofs of this truth as an answer, even if they are superfluous.

As I remarked, if $n \ge 2$ this function is not harmonic at the origin. By the Divergence Theorem, the flux of the gradient of $f$ outward through the boundary of a confined region with smooth boundary is $0$ if $f$ is harmonic in the region. In particular this should be accurate for the region between two spheres centred at the origin. For $f(x) = \|x\|^{2-n}$ the gradient is directed towards the origin (and thus normal to the surface), with magnitude proportional to $\|x\|^{1-n}$. Since the $n-1$-dimensional area of the sphere of radius $r$ is proportional to $r^{n-1}$, that means the flux through the sphere is the same for every $r$, so the flux out of the region between the two spheres is $0$, as it should be.

perturbations.a:
Binomial Theorem Query..

Just revising for my combinatorics assessment. My instructor mentioned there would be a query akin to this one on the assessment, so I'm attempting to solve this one.

$$\sum^{20}_{k=0} \binom{41}{k}$$

I understand if I can extract $\dbinom{20}{k}$ then I can achieve the subsequent:

$$A\sum^{20}_{k=0}\binom{20}{k} * 1^k * 1^{n-k} = A(1+1)^{20}$$

I just am uncertain how to arrive there...

Any assistance is greatly valued!


You’re on the incorrect path, I fear. The secret is to comprehend that your sum is precisely half of the complete sum $\sum_{k=0}^{41}\binom{41}k$ due to the symmetry of the binomial coefficients: $\binom{41}{41-k}=\binom{41}k$.

$$\begin{align*} 2^{41}&=\sum_{k=0}^{41}\binom{41}k\\ &=\sum_{k=0}^{20}\binom{41}k+\sum_{k=21}^{41}\binom{41}k\\ &=\sum_{k=0}^{20}\binom{41}k+\sum_{k=21}^{41}\binom{41}{41-k}\\ &=\sum_{k=0}^{20}\binom{41}k+\sum_{i=0}^{20}\binom{41}i&&\text{set }i=41-k\\ &=2\sum_{k=0}^{20}\binom{41}k\;, \end{align*}$$

so that $$\sum_{k=0}^{20}\binom{41}k=2^{40}\;.$$

perturbations.a:
The pebble arrangement (Bulgarian solitaire)  
  
Let we have $n\cdot(n+1)/2$ rocks grouped by heaps. We can select 1 rock from each heap and place them as a new heap. Show that after doing it some times we will achieve the following heaps: $1, 2, \ldots n$ rocks.  
  
Example: $n = 3$  
  
Let we have 2 heaps with 3 rocks of each.  
  
$$3 3 \to 2 2 2 \to 1 1 1 3 \to 2 4 \to 1 3 2$$  
  
This was originally established by Jørgen Brandt in Cycles of Partitions, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society, Vol. 85, No. 3 (Jul., 1982), pp. 483-486, which is freely accessible here. The verification of this outcome covers the first page and a half and is quite concise.  
  
First note that there are merely finitely many possible sets of heap sizes, so at some instance a position must repeat a former position. Say that $P_{m+p}=P_m$ for some $p>0$, where $P_n$ is the $n$-th position (set of heap sizes) in the game. It’s not difficult to see that the game will then cycle through the positions $P_{m+k}$, $k=0,\dots,p-1$, repeatedly. The verification consists in demonstrating that when there are $\frac12n(n+1)$ pebbles, the sole possible cycle is the one of length one from $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ to $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.  
  
Brian Hopkins, 30 Years of Bulgarian Solitaire, The College Mathematics Journal, Vol. 43, No. 2, March 2012, pp. 135-140, has references to other published verifications; one appears to be to a less accessible version of the document Karatsuba Solitaire (Therese A. Hart, Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan) that MJD found at arXiv.org.  
  
Added: And having now read the Hart, Khan, & Khan article, I concur with MJD: the reasoning is quite straightforward, and it’s presented very well.  
  
Added 28 April 2023: The final published edition of the Hart, Khan, & Khan article is now accessible at arXiv. Vesselin Drensky, The Bulgarian solitaire and the mathematics surrounding it, is also of interest and is also accessible at arXiv.

perturbations.d:
The pebble configuration (Bulgarian solitaire)  
  
Let we have $n\cdot(n+1)/2$ marbles grouped by mounds. We can gather 1 marble from each mound and assemble them as a new mound. Show that after doing it some times we will realize the following mounds: $1, 2, \ldots n$ marbles.  
  
Example: $n = 3$  
  
Let we have 2 mounds with 3 marbles of each.  
  
$$3 3 \to 2 2 2 \to 1 1 1 3 \to 2 4 \to 1 3 2$$  
  
This was originally substantiated by Jørgen Brandt in Cycles of Partitions, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society, Vol. 85, No. 3 (Jul., 1982), pp. 483-486, which is freely obtainable here. The substantiation of this phenomenon covers the first page and a half and is rather concise.  
  
First note that there are solely finitely many possible sets of mound sizes, so at some time a position must repeat a prior position. Say that $P_{m+p}=P_m$ for some $p>0$, where $P_n$ is the $n$-th position (set of mound sizes) in the game. It’s not difficult to ascertain that the game will then cycle through the positions $P_{m+k}$, $k=0,\dots,p-1$, frequently. The substantiation consists in demonstrating that when there are $\frac12n(n+1)$ pebbles, the only existing cycle is the one of length one from $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ to $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.  
  
Brian Hopkins, 30 Years of Bulgarian Solitaire, The College Mathematics Journal, Vol. 43, No. 2, March 2012, pp. 135-140, has references to other published substantiations; one appears to be to a less accessible version of the paper Karatsuba Solitaire (Therese A. Hart, Gabriel Khan, Mizan R. Khan) that MJD found at arXiv.org.  
  
Added: And having now read the Hart, Khan, & Khan manuscript, I side with MJD: the reasoning is quite simple, and it’s presented very well.  
  
Added 28 April 2023: The final published version of the Hart, Khan, & Khan manuscript is now accessible at arXiv. Vesselin Drensky, The Bulgarian solitaire and the mathematics surrounding it, is also of interest and is also accessible at arXiv.
